Now multiply by term frequency, each word's share of its document. Cat is one word in six, so it scores about zero point one eight. The word the is two in six, times zero. The column that led every row drops to zero. At the top of the first document, cat, mat, on and sat tie. On says nothing about cats, but it's just as rare, and rarity is all IDF can see. So TF-IDF rewards words that are frequent here and rare elsewhere, with no stopword list at all.

One caution: that's the textbook formula. Scikit-learn's default smooths it and adds one, so the word the never reaches zero. On these three documents, it even stays on top. Counts and weights describe a text. The last step makes a call on one: is it positive, or negative?

The simplest sentiment classifier is two word lists: seven positive words, and seven negative. Add one for each positive word, take one away for each negative word, and read the sign. I love this movie: positive. This film is terrible: negative. It is not good... positive. The counter sees good, and never reads the not. Counting words one at a time is a bag of words, so it's blind to order, too.

The fix is one flag. A negation like not, no or never switches it on, and the next sentiment word flips its sign. A comma, a full stop, or the word but switches it off again, so a not can't reach into the next clause. Now, it is not good comes out negative. And this is not bad at all comes out positive. The plot was good but the acting was awful? Plus one, minus one... neutral.
